properties.decision:
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL.

⭐⭐ THE HEADLINE: AN ACCEPTED DECISION SET A CONDITION, AND THE CONDITION HAS NOW BEEN MET BY EXACTLY THE EVIDENCE IT ASKED FOR.

dec:ownership-reads-claims-before-adding-an-edge (ACCEPTED, Anthony's word 2026-08-08) says: build the first cut from CLAIMS rather than a new edge, and \"DECIDE ON OWNED_BY ONLY AFTER THAT IS BUILT AND SHOWN TO BE INSUFFICIENT.\" Its rationale names the disqualifying evidence in advance: \"If claims turn out to model the wrong thing (THEY ARE TRANSIENT WORK-IN-HAND, WHILE OWNERSHIP IS DURABLE AND SURVIVES THE SESSION), that is a real distinction and the edge becomes justified on evidence rather than on anticipation.\"

ONE DAY LATER, dev_storyflow filed precisely that distinction, and Anthony supplied the use case himself (2026-08-09, relayed by api-boss 05af57c1):

  \"As my brother and I collaborate on another project, there are areas of the design that are his and areas that are mine. This is probably a different 'ownership' of something than the claim_region type descriptor... it is probably DURABLE, SURVIVES EVERY SESSION, and SHOULD NEVER BE RELEASED.\"

⭐ THE FRAMING THAT MAKES IT LEGIBLE — reflow2 has two of the three WHO axes:
  AUTHORED_BY   who WROTE this          past tense · historical · never changes
  CLAIMS        who is IN it RIGHT NOW  transient · advisory · released at checkout
  ???           whose AREA this is      durable · standing · never released

WHY CLAIMS CANNOT BE STRETCHED TO COVER THE THIRD, which is the \"shown to be insufficient\" the accepted decision demanded, and it is operational rather than theoretical: claim_region's own description says ADVISORY and session-scoped; the parallel-work skill says release at checkout; on a shared server a claim reads `unknown` rather than `live` and NEVER EXPIRES ON ITS OWN. So standing ownership claims would permanently drown the tool's actual job — showing who is ACTIVELY in your ground. api-boss noted they hold one claim, released and re-took it once today purely to fix its note, and asked what three permanent graph-wide claims would do to that surface.

⚠️ AND THE FLEET RETRACTED ITS OWN COUNTER-ARGUMENT, which is worth more than the ask. They had argued that recording ownership in the graph duplicates their PROTOCOL.md ownership matrix and would rot the way six of their copied rules already have. Their retraction: \"That objection is specific to an organisation that ALREADY writes ownership down. A PAIR OF COLLABORATORS HAS NO MATRIX — the knowledge lives in their heads and in habit. For most projects the graph would be the FIRST place ownership was ever recorded, not the second, and the duplication risk is simply absent.\" They kept only the narrow fleet-specific form.

⭐ AND THE REFRAME THAT MATTERS MOST FOR SCOPE: every earlier version of this ask was framed around an AGENT FLEET, which invites the reply \"that is exotica\". The two-person case is not exotica. It is two people splitting a design, which is the ORDINARY case of collaborative design work.

=== WHERE THIS SITS AGAINST WHAT SHIPPED TODAY ===

cap:owed-to-a-contributor shipped `loop_status(contributor_id)` on 2026-08-09. IT IS NOT THE FIRST CUT THAT ACCEPTED DECISION SPECIFIED: it attributes via the AUTHORED_BY `role=approver` edge, not via CLAIMS. That is already recorded honestly — the SATISFIES edge to req:ownership-is-an-edge-so-debt-has-an-addressee carries `coverage: partial` and says so: \"its chosen first cut answers 'what has a named person been asked to settle', not 'which gaps are in the part of the system I own'. The fleet's ask is the second one.\"

⇒ SO THE CLAIMS-BASED FIRST CUT WAS NEVER BUILT, and the question is whether it still should be. Two readings, both honest:
  (a) The decision's build order stands: build the claims-based cut, THEN judge. The insufficiency argument above is about claims as a DURABLE record, and a claims-scoped debt report might still be useful for its actual purpose without ever being ownership.
  (b) The insufficiency is already established by inspection — claims are advisory, session-scoped and released by doctrine, so building a durable ownership view on them would be building on a foundation whose own description forbids it. Under this reading the condition is met and the edge is justified now.

AND IT FITS WHAT SHIPPED: loop_status's scoped answer deliberately attributes ONLY assignment and reports everything else under `scope.not_attributable`. AN OWNED_BY EDGE IS EXACTLY WHAT WOULD LET THE REST BECOME ATTRIBUTABLE. The restraint shipped today is waiting for this.

=== THE SHAPES, with counters beside rather than argued down ===

(A) AN OWNED_BY / ACCOUNTABILITY EDGE — Contributor → any node, explicitly NOT in the decomposition spine and NOT a traceability edge. THE PRECEDENT EXISTS TWICE: AUTHORED_BY and CLAIMS are both already deliberately excluded from impact propagation (nodes.rs structural_rule), so this would be the third of a kind rather than a novelty. COUNTER, and it is this project's own: dec:ownership-reads-claims-before-adding-an-edge warns that adding an edge type is the most expensive and least reversible change to this schema, and today's measurement found EIGHT of sixty edge types declared and reached by nothing. An unused OWNED_BY would not be a novel failure here; it is the common one.

(B) REUSE CLAIMS WITH A DURABILITY FLAG — a `durable: true` property that exempts a claim from release and from the overlap report. Cheapest, no new edge type. COUNTER: it makes one edge mean two things whose lifecycles are opposite, and the tool's descriptions would have to say both. That is how a vocabulary rots — the same sentence dec:one-retire-edge uses about two words for one relationship, running the other way.

(C) OWNERSHIP AS A PROPERTY ON THE NODE — an `owner` field. Cheapest of all to read. COUNTER: it cannot express shared or partial ownership, cannot carry a note about WHAT is owned, and puts a person's id inside design content where every export and every merge has to reconcile it.

⚠️ THE HARD PART, WHICH IS A DESIGN INPUT RATHER THAN A SETTING, and it comes from the fleet: WHICH NODE TYPES ARE OWNABLE? In their 1,127-node graph most nodes legitimately have no owner — \"a Constraint about prose rendering is nobody's in the accountability sense\" — so a naive detector fires on the majority and becomes a signal trained to be ignored. In a two-person project the design is probably mostly partitioned. ⇒ OWNABILITY LOOKS LIKE A PER-PROJECT DECLARATION, NOT A FIXED RULE, and the same feature behaves very differently at those two scales.

NOTHING IS PROMOTED. The accepted decision's condition may now be met; saying so is Anthony's to do, and dec:reopen-supersedes says a re-opening mints its own node rather than un-accepting the old one.
properties.name: OPEN — the condition dec:ownership-reads-claims-before-adding-an-edge set has now been met: are CLAIMS shown insufficient, and does OWNED_BY become justified?
properties.rationale:
Recorded via the brainstorm skill: `proposed`, options with counters, nothing promoted.

Kept SEPARATE from dec:ownership-reads-claims-before-adding-an-edge rather than editing it, because that decision is ACCEPTED and dec:reopen-supersedes is explicit that a re-opening mints a new Decision which obsoletes the old one — the accepted one is never un-accepted. This node is the evidence arriving that its own condition named; whether that closes it is Anthony's call.

Separated from the ownership-orphan detector question (dec:idea-detect-ownership-orphans) because the edge could exist without the detector and the detector cannot exist without the edge — one node holding both could only be half-answered.
